lead: A liquid surface stores energy because molecules at the surface are pulled inward. This stored energy acts like a stretched sheet and is called surface tension. It creates a pressure jump across curved interfaces such as droplets and soap bubbles. It also pulls liquid up or pushes it down in narrow tubes, an effect called capillarity. Engineers meet it in rain drops, inkjet printing, soil water, wicks, manometer tubes and lab pipettes. At small scales it can dominate gravity.
prereq: You need density and specific weight from Ch 1.2; pressure in a static fluid is covered in Ch 1.6.

sections.h3: Surface tension: force per unit length

blocks.text: Inside a liquid, each molecule is pulled equally in all directions by its neighbours. At the free surface there are no molecules above, so the net pull is inward. The surface therefore behaves like a stretched sheet. Surface tension σ is the force per unit length along any line drawn on the surface.

blocks.where: σ is surface tension in N/m; F is the force in N acting along a line of length L in m on the surface.

blocks.text: The same σ is the surface energy per unit area, in J/m². Values are small but not negligible at small scales. For water at 20 °C, σ ≈ 0.072 N/m; for mercury, σ ≈ 0.48 N/m. Surface tension falls as temperature rises because faster molecular motion weakens the inward pull. Soap lowers the surface tension of water. Small droplets become spherical because a sphere has the least surface area for a given volume.

sections.h3: Pressure jump across a curved surface

blocks.text: A curved liquid surface is stretched, so it pushes inward. For a droplet of radius R in a gas, the pressure inside is higher than outside.

blocks.where: Δp is the pressure difference in Pa; σ is surface tension in N/m; R is the droplet radius in m.

blocks.text: A soap bubble in air has two surfaces, an inner one and an outer one, so the pressure jump doubles.

blocks.where: for a soap bubble in air; R is the bubble radius in m. A bubble inside a liquid has one surface, so use 2σ/R.

blocks.text: Smaller R gives a larger Δp. A water droplet of radius 1 mm has Δp = 2 × 0.072 / 0.001 = 144 Pa; one of radius 0.1 mm has Δp = 1440 Pa. This is why tiny droplets resist being squashed.

The contact angle θ is the angle, inside the liquid, between the tube wall and the tangent to the liquid surface at the contact line. If θ < 90°, the liquid wets the wall and the meniscus is concave; water on clean glass has θ ≈ 0°. If θ > 90°, it does not wet the wall and the meniscus is convex; mercury on glass has θ ≈ 140°.
In a capillary tube of internal radius r, surface tension pulls the liquid up along the contact line. The raised liquid column has weight, and the two balance.

items: The vertical component of surface tension per unit length is σ cosθ.
The contact line length is 2πr, so the upward force is 2πrσ cosθ.
The weight of the raised column is ρgπr²h.
Equate and cancel πr: 2σ cosθ = ρgrh.

blocks.where: h is capillary rise in m; σ is surface tension in N/m; θ is contact angle in degrees; ρ is liquid density in kg/m³; g is gravitational acceleration in m/s²; r is internal tube radius in m.

blocks.text: If θ > 90°, cosθ is negative, so h is negative: the liquid is depressed. Mercury sinks in a narrow glass tube. The same formula gives the depression. Use the internal radius, not the diameter. A narrower tube gives a larger rise because h is proportional to 1/r.

figure.caption: Surface tension at a liquid surface produces a pressure jump across a curved interface and pulls liquid up a narrow tube; notice the factor 2 for a droplet and 4 for a soap bubble.

spec.title: Surface tension effects

nodes.label: Capillary rise
nodes.note: 2.94 cm in a tube of radius 0.5 mm

spec.aria: Surface tension creates a pressure jump in droplets and soap bubbles and drives capillary rise in a narrow tube.

examples.question: A clean glass capillary tube of internal radius 0.5 mm is dipped in water. Take σ = 0.072 N/m, θ = 0°, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find the capillary rise h in metres and centimetres.
steps: Convert the radius: r = 0.5 mm = 0.5 × 10⁻³ m = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m.
The contact angle is 0°, so cosθ = cos0° = 1.
examples.answer: The water rises by h ≈ 0.0294 m, or 2.94 cm, in the 0.5 mm radius tube.
examples.check:
import math
sigma = 0.072
theta_deg = 0.0
rho = 1000.0
g = 9.81
r = 0.5e-3
h = 2 * sigma * math.cos(math.radians(theta_deg)) / (rho * g * r)
print(round(h, 4))
print(round(h * 100, 2))

traps: Using 2σ/R for a soap bubble. A soap film has two surfaces, so the pressure jump is 4σ/R.
Using diameter in place of radius. The formula needs the internal radius r; halve the diameter first.
Putting θ in the cosine without checking its meaning. θ is measured inside the liquid, and cosθ is negative for mercury, giving a depression.
Forgetting that σ falls with temperature. A value of 0.072 N/m is for water near 20 °C, not for hot water.
Ignoring capillarity in narrow manometer tubes. A small tube can shift the reading; wide tubes reduce this error.

quiz.q: Define surface tension and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Surface tension is the force per unit length along a line on a liquid surface. Its SI unit is N/m. Numerically it equals the surface energy in J/m².

quiz.q: Why is the pressure inside a small droplet higher than the pressure outside?
quiz.a: The curved surface is stretched and pushes inward like a membrane. The inside pressure must be higher by Δp = 2σ/R to balance this inward push.

quiz.q: A soap bubble in air has radius 2 cm and surface tension σ = 0.025 N/m. Find the pressure difference across the film.
quiz.a: R = 0.02 m. For a soap bubble, Δp = 4σ/R = 4 × 0.025 / 0.02 = 5 Pa.

quiz.q: A capillary tube radius is halved. What happens to the water rise h, and why?
quiz.a: h doubles. The upward force is proportional to r, while the weight of the column is proportional to r², so h is proportional to 1/r.

quiz.q: Mercury in a glass tube: r = 1 mm, θ = 140°, σ = 0.48 N/m, ρ = 13600 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find h.
quiz.a: h = 2 × 0.48 × cos140° / (13600 × 9.81 × 0.001) = −0.00551 m = −5.51 mm. The negative sign means depression.

quiz.q: Why does a soap bubble have 4σ/R while a droplet has 2σ/R?
quiz.a: A soap film has two surfaces, inner and outer. Each surface gives a jump 2σ/R, so the total is 4σ/R. A droplet has only one surface.

quiz.q: How does surface tension change with temperature?
quiz.a: Surface tension falls as temperature rises.

beyond: Not for the exam. Surface tension gradients drive Marangoni flow, used in crystal growth and in the tears of wine. Surfactants change σ and stabilise emulsions in food and paint. Microfluidic chips use capillary pressure and the capillary number Ca = μU/σ to predict droplet breakup. Enhanced oil recovery uses surfactants to lower interfacial tension. Search Young–Laplace equation, capillary number and Marangoni effect.
